extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining 35 U.S.C. §101 subject-matter eligibility of claims that recite or involve laws of nature, natural phenomena, or natural products, using a factors-based analysis (factors a–l) and illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor a) — Markedly different product
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the natural products recited in the claim are 'markedly different' from what exists in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the recited natural product is structurally or functionally altered in a way that is significant relative to its natural counterpart, factor a) may be satisfied. Examples and counterexamples: isolated nucleic acids may have minor structural changes (broken bonds) but lack significant functional differences and thus may not be 'markedly different' (see Myriad discussion); bacteria unchanged from nature are not markedly different. Use specification/record to assess whether the product has been meaningfully altered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor b) — Additional elements meaningfully limit claim scope (not foreclose others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether elements in addition to the judicial exception narrow the scope of the claim so that others are not substantially foreclosed from using the natural products in other ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfied when claimed additional elements impose specific limitations (e.g., defined temperatures, times, steps, particular physical integration) that leave substantial alternative uses of the natural products open to others. Example: thermal cycling steps that limit amplification to a particular protocol meaningfully limit scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor c) — Elements relate to the natural products in a significant way
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claimed elements relate to the natural products in a significant (more than insignificant or tangential) way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfied when elements directly manipulate or integrate natural products (e.g., forming a structure that physically integrates natural products, or steps that directly manipulate the products). Use the nature of the relationship (physical integration, direct manipulation) to judge significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor d) — Claimed elements do more than describe with general instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claimed elements do more than merely describe the natural products with general instructions to use or apply them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfied when the claim recites a specific practical application (e.g., a firework assembly including particular components; use of a particular antibody and detection method) rather than abstract/general instructions. If only a general instruction to apply the principle is recited, factor d) is not satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor e) — Machine-or-transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a machine is recited or a transformation is performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor e) is satisfied if the claim includes a recited machine or a transformation; if neither is recited, factor e) is not satisfied. Use this factor where applicable to identify tangible machines/transformations in the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor f) — Additional elements are more than well-understood, purely conventional, or routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the additional claimed elements add anything more than what is well-understood, purely conventional, or routine in the relevant art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfied when the specification/record shows that an additional element is not routine or conventional (e.g., a newly created antibody). If the added elements are routine/conventional in the art (e.g., standard heating and cooling steps in PCR), factor f) is not satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor g) — Natural products are not markedly different (weighs against eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the recited natural products are not markedly different from their natural counterparts, a factor that weighs against eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If natural products are structurally and functionally the same as in nature, factor g) is satisfied (weighs against significant difference). This is the counterpart to factor a) on the 'against' side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor h) — Claim recited at high level of generality covering substantially all practical applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claimed elements are recited at such a high level of generality that the claim covers substantially all practical applications of the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfied when claim language is broad enough to preempt substantially all uses (e.g., broad instruction to expose to sunlight) and thus weighs against eligibility. If specific limitations prevent coverage of substantially all practical applications, factor h) is not satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor i) — Claimed elements are required for use of the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claimed elements are required to apply or use the natural products/principle (i.e., whether everyone who uses the judicial exception would be required to use the claimed elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim forces everyone using the natural product/principle to employ the claimed additional elements, factor i) is satisfied (weighs against eligibility). If alternative means exist (e.g., different antibodies or detection methods), factor i) is not satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor j) — Additional elements are well-understood, purely conventional, routine (weighs against eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the additional elements are well-understood, purely conventional, and routine in the art, which weighs against eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the recited additional steps or components are routine in the field (e.g., standard PCR cycling, using conventional detection techniques), factor j) is satisfied and counts against eligibility. If the added element is novel/non-routine (e.g., novel antibody), factor j) is not satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor k) — Additional elements are insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the elements in addition to the judicial exception are merely insignificant extra-solution activity (do not integrate the exception into a practical application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfied when the additional elements are merely appended steps or conventional activity that do not meaningfully integrate the exception. Not satisfied when steps integrate the exception (e.g., direct manipulation, specific positioning/filtering).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor l) — Mere field-of-use or attempt to limit to a particular technological environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claimed elements are merely a field-of-use limitation or an attempt to limit application of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfied when the claim simply restricts use to a particular field or environment without adding a meaningful inventive application (e.g., limiting white light principle to treatment of mood disorder using sunlight alone). Such limitations count against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply factors per claim type (process vs product)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the factors according to whether the claim is to a product (manufacture/composition) or a process; some factors (e.g., a and g) are not relevant to process claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing process claims, factors a and g (about product being 'markedly different') are not relevant. Other factors (b–f, h–l) remain applicable but must be interpreted in context (e.g., whether steps meaningfully limit scope, integrate the principle, are conventional). Use examples in guidance: process claims with thermal cycling satisfied b, c, d but not e/f in example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall balancing test — 'significantly different' determination
rubrics_metrics.description: After evaluating factors toward and against eligibility, balance them to determine whether the claim as a whole recites something 'significantly different' than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the factors weigh toward 'significantly different', the claim qualifies as eligible subject matter; if they weigh against, the claim does not qualify. Apply all relevant factors and consider specification/record evidence when balancing. Examples: manufacture/composition claims with integrated, specific elements may weigh toward eligibility; pure compositions of natural products often weigh against.

rubrics_metrics.name: When claim recites an abstract idea and a natural product — follow MPEP §2106(II)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites both an abstract idea and a natural product, analyze Question 3 using only the guidance in MPEP §2106(II), which controls the practical-application analysis for abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate analyses — the handling of abstract ideas is controlled by §2106(II). Use that section's guidance about applying/practical-application of judicial exceptions when the claim includes an abstract idea (see H example regarding BRCA2 sequence comparison).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraph ¶7.05.13 for 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Revised form paragraph 7.05.13 is to be used when rejecting claims (machine, composition, manufacture, or process claims) that recite or involve a law of nature/natural principle, natural phenomenon, or natural product for lack of subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ¶7.05.13 language: 'the claimed invention is not directed to patent eligible subject matter. Based upon an analysis with respect to the claim as a whole, claim(s) [1] do not recite something significantly different than a judicial exception. The rationale for this determination is explained below: [2]'. Examiner Note: this form paragraph should be used when rejecting claim(s) that have a law of nature/natural principle or a natural phenomenon, e.g., a natural product, as a claim limitation. Must be preceded by form paragraphs 7.04 and 7.05.
